dataset.name: Chamber Flux and Porewater Concentration of CH4, CO2 and N2O, 2018, Columbia River bank at the Hanford site, WA, USA
description: This is the corresponding observations data for the paper: Jorge A Villa; Garrett J Smith; Yang Ju; Lupita Renteria; Jordan C Angle; Evan Arntzen; Samuel F Harding; Huiying Ren; Xingyuan Chen; Audrey H Sawyer; Emily B Graham; James C Stegen; Kelly C Wrighton; Gil Bohrer (2020) Methane and nitrous oxide porewater concentrations and surface fluxes of a regulated river. Science of the Total Environment.

Greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from rivers are a critical missing component of current global GHG models. Their exclusion is mainly due to a lack of in-situ measurements and a poor understanding of the spatiotemporal dynamics of GHG production and emissions, which prevents optimal model parametrization. We combined simultaneous observations of porewater concentrations along different beach positions and depths, and surface fluxes of methane and nitrous oxide at a plot scale in a large regulated river during three water stages: rising, falling, and low. Our goal was to gain insights into the interactions between hydrological exchanges and GHG emissions and elucidate possible hypotheses that could guide future research on the mechanisms of GHG production, consumption, and transport in the hyporheic zone (HZ). Results indicate that the site functioned as a net source of methane. Surface fluxes of methane during river water stages at three beach positions (shallow, intermediate and deep) correlated with porewater concentrations of methane. However, fluxes were significantly higher in the intermediate position during the low water stage, suggesting that low residence time increased methane emissions. Vertical profiles of methane peaked at different depths, indicating an influence of the magnitude and direction of the hyporheic mixing during the different river water stages on methane production and consumption. The site acted as either a sink or a source of nitrous oxide depending on the elevation of the water column. Nitrous oxide porewater concentrations peaked at the upper layers of the sediment throughout the different water stages. River hydrological stages significantly influenced porewater concentrations and fluxes of GHG, probably by influencing heterotrophic respiration (production and consumption processes) and transport to and from the HZ. Our results highlight the importance of including dynamic hydrological exchanges when studying and modeling GHG production and consumption in the HZ of large rivers.

spatialCoverage.description: Hanford site, operated by Pacific Northwest Laboratory, Richland, WA. Fixed sample locations along the bank of the Columbia River. The samples were collected in the 'Genome to Greenhouse observatory (3G) observatory, a 6- x 11-m (width x length) plot on the beach of the river in the 300 Area. The 3G observatory consists of an array of 3 triplicate porewater samplers (peepers) deployed at a sandy beach on bank-to-river transects along a microtopographic gradient representing three nominal beach positions: shallow, intermediate and deep. The plot is located in a small cove that isolates the site from the flow influence of the main river channel. Water levels in the Columbia River at the 300 Area is highly influenced by upstream river regulation of the Priest River Dam. Water levels can fluctuate in the site up to 0.5 meters intra-daily variations during low water stages in the river (late summer to early spring). Peepers in shallow and intermediate positions during periods of low river water stage and high fluctuation, experience frequent cycles of drying and rewetting.

measurementTechnique:
Porewater Dissolved CO2, CH4 and N2O Concentration Measurements: Peeper
Porewater samples for determining CO2, CH4 concentrations were collected using in-situ dialysis samplers (peepers) described by MacDonald et al. (2013), following the procedure described in Angle et al. (2017). The peepers feature 20 stacked (61.4 ml) cells at a 2.8 cm vertical resolution. Each cell has a (22.5 cm2) windows covered with a 0.22 µm membrane that allows the water inside the cell to equilibrate with dissolved gas concentrations in the sediments. Cells were fitted with two sampling ports consisting of plastic tubing that allowed water extraction and refill. We sampled ten cells, starting at the top cell (at zero sediment depth) and every other after that, until reaching the bottom-most cell at 50-cm sediment depth. At each sampling, a 10 ml water sample was extracted from each cell through one tubing, while the other tubing remained connected to a container with N2 to avoid oxygen intrusion. After the sample extraction, the cell was refilled with deionized water degassed with N2. Samples were placed in 10 ml container pre-acidified with 0.2 ml HCl 2M, refrigerated and transported to the laboratory for further processing.
In the laboratory, dissolved CO2, CH4 and N2O concentrations were determined using the Gas chromatography headspace equilibration technique described by (Kampbell et al., 1989). We equilibrated subsamples of 5-ml of sampled water with a 15-ml N2 headspace. Upon equilibration, we injected 10 ml of headspace into 10-ml pre-evacuated vials and analyzed them in a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014, Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with a flame ionization detector fitted with a 1.8 Poropack Q column and an electron capture Ni-63 detector. Helium (25 ml min-1) was used as the carrier gas for methane and CO2 analysis and ultra-pure N2 (10 ml min-1) was used as the carrier gas for N2O analysis. We included CO2, CH4 and N2O check standards every 20 samples to ensure that the chromatograph maintained the calibration throughout the analysis. If the deviation between the measured value and the value of the check standard was greater than 10%, we recalibrated the chromatograph and re-ran the samples.
We calculated CO2, CH4 and N2O molar concentrations (mC) in the liquid phase, from the measured gas concentrations in the headspace as:
mC = (p_i/RT*Vh+p_i/H_i *Vl)/Vl (1)
Where p_i is the partial pressure of CO2, CH4 or N2O (Headspace concentration (ppm) × ambient pressure at room conditions (0.010325 MPa)), R is the universal gas constant (0.008314 (L MPa K-1 mol-1), T is the room temperature (K), Vh is the volume of the headspace (ml), H_i is the Henry’s volatility constant for each gas (2.96, 67.13, 3.82 L Mpa mol-1, for CO2 and methane respectively), and Vl the volume of the liquid subsample used to create the headspace (ml).

N2O Flux from Chamber Measurements: Manual/Shimadzu
We used closed, non-steady state chambers to sample N2O at each peeper location. The chambers had the same dimensions and the same features as the chambers used to sample CO2 and CH4, in addition to a 20 mm grey butyl stopper in the top that served as a sampling port, and a 3-m long Tygon tubing (1.6 mm internal diameter) for pressure relief. During each chamber deployment (24 min each), 7 gas samples were extracted every 4 minutes with a syringe and placed in 10 ml pre-evacuated vials. The vials were analyzed later in the laboratory with a gas chromatograph (Shimadzu GC-2014, Shimadzu Scientific Instruments, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with an electron capture Ni-63 detector. We used ultra-pure N2 (10 ml min-1) as the carrier gas for N2O analysis. We included N2O check standards every 20 samples to ensure that the chromatograph maintained the calibration throughout the analysis. If the deviation between the measured value and the value of the check standard was greater than 10%, we recalibrated the chromatograph and re-ran the samples.
Mass/volume concentrations of samples were calculated using a modified gas law, following the procedure described in Holland et al. (1999):
Cm= (Cv*P)/(R*T) (2)
where Cm is the mass/volume concentration of the gas (i.e. nmol N2O m-3), Cv is the volume (ppm) of gas, P is atmospheric pressure (Pa), R is the universal gas constant (8.314 m3 Pa mol-1K-1), and T is the air temperature (K) of the chamber.
The accumulation rate (Crate) was determined using the slope of the linear regression fitted to the time points collected for each chamber. The flux rate (F_manual, nmol N2O m-2 s-1) was calculated as:
F_manual = (V*C_rate)/A (3)
where V is volume of chamber (m^3), C_rate is the accumulation rate in nmol N2O m-3 s-1, and A is area of soil surface (m^2).

CO2 and CH4 Flux from Chamber Measurements: Picarro Gas Scouter
At each peeper location, CO2 and CH4 fluxes were determined simultaneously by cavity ring-down spectroscopy using a portable greenhouse gas analyzer (Gas Scouter G4301, Picarro, Santa Clara, CA) coupled to custom made transparent polyethylene dome-shaped chambers. The chambers (7.3 × 10-2 m2 surface area, 7.7 × 10-3 m3 volume) were equipped with a thermometer to record temperatures inside the chamber during deployment, and had a 12v fan for air mixing. The chambers recirculated at a flow rate of 1 L min-1, and recorded the CO2 and CH4 concentrations at a frequency of 1 Hz. Three replicates of chamber deployments were conducted consecutively at each peeper location.
In each chamber measurement, we fitted a 3-minute, 1 Hz time series of CO2 and CH4 concentrations, C_HM (µmol mol -1), to the non-linear Hutchinson and Moiser one-dimension diffusion model (Hutchinson & Mosier, 1981; Kutzbach et al., 2007; Pedersen et al., 2010):
C_HM=CS+ (C0- CS ) *e^(-kt) (4)
Where C0 is the pre-deployment concentration of methane or CO2 (µmol mol-1), Cs is the constant source or sink concentration (µmol mol-1), and k is a curve shape parameter (s-1). C0, Cs, and k are parameters determined by fitting the observed gas concentrations in the chamber over time, t (s). We then calculated the flux, F_Diff, of methane and CO2, (µmol m-2 s-1) at the wetland surface as:
F_Diff =k *(C0- CS)*pV/RTchA (5)
Where p (kPa) is the atmospheric pressure, measured with a manual barometer at the site; V the volume of the chamber (m^3), R the universal gas constant (0.0083145 m^3 kPa mol-1 K-1), Tch the temperature inside the chamber (K), A the surface area enclosed in the chamber (m^2).

Sampling design
The sampling was conducted along a triplicated bank-to-river transect on the Columbia River, Handford Reach (Handford 300 Area), Washington State, USA (Figure 1). The transects were 6 m long and represented three nominal positions: shallow, intermediate and deep. The transects encompassed an 11-m long plot. During flux measurements, chambers were secured manually (Picarro chambers) or by attaching them to the PVC pipes that house the peeper tubbing (N2O) (Figure 2).

Figure 1 Caption. (A) General location of the study site in Washington State, USA (black square) and river location on the Handford Reach, Handford 300 Area, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. (B) Peeper arrangement showing the three transects sampled for porewater concentration and surface fluxes.
Figure 2 Caption. Chamber positioning approach. (A) installed peeper featuring the PVC pipe to house the sampling tubing. (B) positioning and securing of the methane sampling chamber. (C) positioning and anchoring of the N2O sampling chambers.
